title: Phase 1 — ML Foundations (fast pass)
hours: ~20 hours · fill the gaps, don't redo what you know

weeks.title: Gap Analysis & ML Refresh
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · audit yourself against the ML + Post-ML roadmaps
weeks.mindset:
You already walked the ML and Post-ML roadmaps — this week is an audit, not a re-watch. Skim the Andrew Ng specialization week titles and the Post-ML evaluation/MLOps weeks. Anything you cannot explain cold goes on a personal gap list; everything else is done. The gap list becomes your Phase 1 content.

Prerequisite: complete (or test out of) the /ml-roadmap and /post-ml-roadmap trackers first. This track builds directly on RAG, agents, evaluation, and MLOps — it does not re-teach them.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you have a written gap list against the ML and Post-ML trackers and have closed the two most important gaps.

tasks.content: Skim every week title in the ML specialization and write a one-line summary of each from memory. Where you draw a blank, mark it.
Repeat for the Post-ML phases: evaluation, data engineering, MLOps, transformers, RAG, agents.
Write the gap list: topics you cannot explain cold, ranked by how often they appear in healthcare AI work.
Close gap #1: study it properly — don't just re-watch. Solve one exercise or rebuild one notebook output from scratch.
Write a 5-line explanation of gap #1 for a hospital IT colleague with no ML background. If you can't, you haven't closed it.
Close gap #2 the same way: study, rebuild one artifact, explain in plain words.
Skim scikit-learn pipelines + ColumnTransformer — healthcare data is messy tables, and pipelines are the hygienic way to preprocess them.
Load a public hospital dataset (e.g. MIMIC-IV demo or a Kaggle readmission set). Build a preprocessing sklearn Pipeline: missing-value imputation, scaling, one-hot encoding.
Fit a baseline logistic regression on 30-day readmission. Record AUROC — this baseline number follows you into Phase 3.
Ship the readmission baseline as a small FastAPI /predict endpoint in Docker. You built this on Post-ML — here it runs on healthcare-shaped data.
Add one evaluation report (confusion matrix + AUROC + calibration curve) as an HTML artifact.
Review the gap list: what's closed, what stays open, and whether any open gap blocks Phase 2.
Write the weekly journal: your readmission baseline AUROC and the two gaps you closed.

weeks.title: Deep Learning & Transformers Refresh
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · only the parts healthcare AI leans on
weeks.mindset: Healthcare NLP is embeddings all the way down. Clinical notes, ICD codes, lab panels, patient journeys — every one of them becomes a vector before any model sees it. This week you re-derive the embedding mental model and check your PyTorch and transformer fluency.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can explain embeddings, attention, and fine-tuning trade-offs without notes, and have fine-tuned one small model on clinical text.

tasks.content: Re-derive attention from memory: Q, K, V, why the scaling by √d, why softmax. Then explain embeddings to a clinician in 3 sentences.
Read one survey of clinical language models (ClinicalBERT lineage and successors) — you need to know they exist and what they're pre-trained on.
Study tokenization on clinical text: why BERT wordpieces butcher drug names and abbreviations, and why domain-specific vocabularies exist.
Skim HuggingFace tokenizers docs: train a small WordPiece tokenizer on synthetic clinical notes just to see the vocabulary it learns.
Fine-tune a small pre-trained model (e.g. DistilBERT) on a clinical classification task — public n2c2/i2b2-style de-identified notes or the PubMedQA dataset.
Log runs in MLflow (you already run this stack from Post-ML): baseline vs fine-tuned F1 on the held-out split.
Study when to fine-tune vs prompt vs RAG: cost, latency, data requirement, and the audit story each one gives a hospital review board.
Read one LLM-for-clinical-text evaluation paper: note the metrics (F1, AUROC, hallucination rate) and how the eval set was built.
Wrap the fine-tuned classifier as a FastAPI service with a /explain endpoint returning token-level attention or SHAP-style evidence.
Write a model card: intended use, training data, metrics, failure modes. This artifact reappears in Phase 6.
Journal: the fine-tune delta you measured, and the one clinical-NLP gotcha that surprised you most.

title: Phase 2 — Stanford AI in Healthcare
hours: ~30 hours · domain knowledge that makes the tech useful

weeks.title: AI in Healthcare — Foundations
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · Course 1 of the Stanford specialization
weeks.mindset: The hard part of healthcare AI is rarely the model. It's the workflow, the data, and the trust. Stanford's specialization exists to teach technologists the context: who acts on the prediction, what breaks in a clinical workflow, and why a correct prediction nobody uses saves zero lives.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can describe the modern healthcare data stack (EHR, claims, labs, imaging) and where AI legitimately creates value in it.

tasks.content: Start AI in Healthcare (Stanford, Coursera). Watch the framing lectures: what problems healthcare actually has, and where ML already works (and where it famously doesn't).
Write a one-page map of your own hospital's data reality: which systems exist (EMR/ERP), what data they hold, who owns access.
Continue the course: healthcare data — EHR structure, claims data, the messy reality of codes and free text.
Learn the vocabulary you'll be judged on: ICD-10, CPT, SNOMED CT, LOINC, HL7/FHIR. One flashcard each: what it codes, who uses it.
Study FHIR resources in practice: Patient, Observation, Encounter, Condition. Pull from a public HAPI FHIR test server with Python.
Map 5 fields from a FHIR Observation to a flat ML feature row. This is the daily reality of healthcare ML engineering.
Continue the course: clinical workflow integration — where predictions surface, who acts on them, alert fatigue, and the graveyard of unused clinical decision support.
Pick one workflow in your own workplace and write the integration point: who would see an AI output, in which screen, deciding what.
Finish course weeks on ethics, bias, and fairness in healthcare AI. Note one published example of a biased clinical algorithm and its root cause.
Write your own one-page position: what would make you refuse to deploy a healthcare AI system.
Journal: the three healthcare-data facts that most changed how you'd architect an AI system.

weeks.title: Clinical NLP & Predictive Analytics
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · where your GenAI skills meet the domain
weeks.mindset: Clinical NLP is the highest-leverage intersection of your existing skills and healthcare. 80% of clinical data is unstructured text — notes, referrals, discharge summaries. The models you already know how to build, evaluate, and deploy become dramatically more valuable pointed at that text.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you have built and evaluated one clinical NLP pipeline end to end on public data.

tasks.content: Stanford course: NLP in healthcare weeks — clinical information extraction, named entity recognition on notes, negation detection (“no evidence of pneumonia” is the classic trap).
List the top failure modes of vanilla NLP on clinical text: abbreviations, negation, temporality, copy-forward text.
Build a clinical NER pipeline on the n2c2/i2b2-style public corpora (or synthetic notes): extract medication + dosage + frequency.
Add negation handling — a rule-based NegEx-style pass. Measure how much it changes your extraction precision.
Stanford course: predictive analytics — sepsis early warning, deterioration scores, readmission. Why AUROC alone lied in the famous sepsis-model failures.
Learn the alert economics of clinical prediction: PPV at your prevalence, alerts per clinician per shift, and alert fatigue as the real deployment constraint.
Take your Week 1 readmission model and add clinical-text features (note-derived embeddings or extracted entities). Measure the delta vs the tabular baseline.
Compute the operating point a charge nurse would actually accept: at what threshold do you generate < N alerts/day at PPV > 0.3?
Ship the combined model behind the FastAPI service from Week 1. Version the model artifact in MLflow; the API loads by model version.
Write the eval report: AUROC, PPV at operating point, calibration, and a per-subgroup fairness slice.
Journal: text-feature delta, your operating point, and what the fairness slice showed.

weeks.title: Safety, Bias & Responsible Deployment
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · the material that makes you hirable
weeks.mindset:
In healthcare, the safety review is the product. A model that can't pass governance doesn't ship, no matter its AUROC. This week you learn the regulatory and ethical landscape — and build the artifacts (model cards, audit trails) that review boards ask for.

SaMD awareness: Software as a Medical Device rules (FDA/CE-MDR, and equivalents) determine whether a system needs regulatory clearance. Stay non-diagnostic, informational, or internal-QI unless you explicitly enter that path — and know which side of the line you're on.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can classify a project as SaMD or non-SaMD, run a subgroup fairness audit, and produce a deployment-risk document.

tasks.content: Stanford course: fairness and bias weeks in depth. Study one documented biased-algorithm failure (e.g. the 2019 Obermeyer-style case using cost as a proxy for need).
Learn the three standard fairness lenses: group parity, calibration, and error-rate balance — and why you can't have all three at once.
Run a subgroup fairness audit on your readmission model: AUROC and PPV sliced by age band, sex, and insurance type (or their public-dataset proxies).
Use Fairlearn or a small pandas slice-and-score script. Document the worst gap and one mitigation you'd propose.
Study SaMD classification basics: what makes software a medical device, risk classes, and what “non-diagnostic decision support” means.
Classify your three portfolio projects-to-be: SaMD or not? Write one paragraph of justification each.
Study HIPAA technical safeguards: PHI identifiers, the Safe Harbor de-identification list, minimum necessary, and BAAs when any third-party model API touches PHI.
Write the PHI map for your portfolio stack: every field that is PHI, every place it flows, every control on it.
Produce the deployment-risk pack for the readmission service: model card, fairness audit, PHI map, rollback plan, monitoring plan.
Claim the Stanford AI in Healthcare certificate (finish remaining quizzes). Add it next to the ML Specialization certificate.
Journal: the worst fairness gap you found, and whether your projects are SaMD. These answers shape Phase 4 scoping.

title: Phase 3 — Healthcare AI Portfolio Projects
hours: ~40 hours · the portfolio that gets you the job

weeks.title: Project 1 — Hospital Knowledge Assistant (RAG)
weeks.mindset: In a hospital, an uncited answer is worse than no answer. Your GenAI RAG skills transfer directly — but the bar moves: every sentence must trace to a source document, access control follows the user, and PHI never leaves the boundary. You already know RAG; this week is RAG under hospital constraints.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday a deployed RAG assistant answers policy questions with inline citations and a feedback button, on synthetic policies.

tasks.content: Assemble a corpus of synthetic hospital policies (~50 docs: infection control, HR, IT, pharmacy). Never use real documents.
Design the pipeline you already know: ingestion → chunking → embeddings → hybrid retrieval → rerank → grounded generation with citations.
Build ingestion + chunking with metadata: doc id, section, version, effective date — versioned policy is a real hospital problem.
Embed and load into Qdrant (your Post-ML stack). BM25 + dense hybrid retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion.
Generation with inline citations: every claim links to doc + section. Refusal behavior when retrieval confidence is low.
Add the access-control layer: role-filtered retrieval (an HR doc is invisible to a generic query). Test with two roles.
Evaluation, your Post-ML way: 30-question gold set, precision@k + faithfulness (RAGAS), before/after reranking.
Add feedback capture: thumbs up/down + comment, stored per answer for future fine-tuning data.
Deploy: FastAPI + Docker, PHI boundary documented (synthetic data now, real contract later). Simple chat UI or CLI.
Write the project README like a case study: problem, constraints, architecture, eval numbers, what you'd do with real data.
Journal: eval numbers, the retrieval failure that surprised you, and the one feature you'd pitch to a hospital committee.

weeks.title: Project 2 — Operations Analytics Assistant
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · SQL + LLM over hospital ops data
weeks.mindset: This project is your 8 years of hospital ERP experience, weaponized. Text-to-SQL over an operational star schema, with an LLM summarizing and explaining trends — the exact intersection where you outshine generic AI engineers with no domain background.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday a deployed assistant answers natural-language ops questions over a synthetic hospital warehouse with verified SQL and trend narratives.

tasks.content: Design a synthetic hospital ops warehouse (DuckDB or Postgres): encounters, departments, appointments, no-shows, length-of-stay. Seeded, versioned, documented.
Load a month of synthetic data with realistic skew (weekday/weekend, seasonal, department variation).
Build text-to-SQL with guardrails: schema-aware prompting, read-only credentials, generated-SQL validation, row/time limits.
Curate a 25-question eval set with gold SQL. Measure execution accuracy — the honest text-to-SQL metric.
Add narrative summaries: LLM turns query results into a 3-bullet ops briefing with the numbers cited from the result set.
Add bottleneck detection: assistant flags anomalies (no-show spike, LOS drift) and explains candidate causes with the data.
Wire the eval into CI from Post-ML: 25-question suite gates the PR; execution accuracy below threshold blocks merge.
Add query cost logging: tokens, latency, and warehouse scan size per question.
Deploy behind FastAPI with a minimal analytics UI. Write the case-study README — lead with your hospital-ERP domain angle.
Record a 3-minute demo: ask three ops questions, show verified SQL, trend narrative, and anomaly flag.
Journal: execution-accuracy number, worst failure category, and what domain knowledge contributed that a generic prompter would miss.

weeks.title: Project 3 — Workflow Agent with Human Approval
weeks.mindset: Autonomy is a dial, and in healthcare it starts near zero. Your Post-ML agent skills apply, but every consequential action routes through a human. The interesting engineering is the gate: state, review UI, approval semantics, and the audit log that governance will ask for.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday a deployed agent drafts a real workflow artifact, routes it for human approval, and logs every decision.

tasks.content: Pick the workflow: incident-report drafting from ops events (great fit for your ERP background) or discharge-summary structuring.
Design the agent graph: read events → retrieve context → draft → human gate → commit + notify. Draw it before you code it.
Build the LangGraph flow with a checkpointed human-in-the-loop node (interrupt before commit).
Tools: warehouse query (read-only), document retrieval (Project 1's index), draft submission (gated). MCP or plain tools — your call.
Build the review UI: pending drafts queue, diff view, approve/reject-with-reason. Reject reason feeds the next iteration.
Implement the audit trail: every state transition, tool call, approval, and rejection persisted — immutable, queryable.
Add agent evaluation: 10 scenario tasks scored on draft quality, correct gating, and zero unapproved commits.
Test the failure paths deliberately: tool error mid-flow, reviewer timeout, malformed draft. Each must land in a safe state.
Deploy the full stack. Write the README emphasizing the governance story — this is the artifact that differentiates you.
Record a 3-minute demo: event stream in, draft produced, human approves, audit trail queried.
Journal: where the agent saved time, where the human gate earned its cost, and what you'd automate next.

weeks.title: Project 4 — Patient Flow Prediction
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · classical ML on real operational problems
weeks.mindset: Not everything in 2026 is an LLM. ED demand, no-shows, and length-of-stay are tabular forecasting problems where gradient boosting still beats deep learning — and where your Andrew Ng diagnostics training decides whether the model helps or hallucinates trend.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday a deployed forecasting service predicts ED demand and no-show risk with drift monitoring live.

tasks.content: Extend the Week 7 warehouse with a year of synthetic ED arrivals + appointments with realistic seasonality, holidays, and epidemic bumps.
Define the prediction tasks precisely: next-24h ED arrivals by hour; no-show probability per appointment; LOS category per admission.
Feature engineering: lag features, rolling windows, calendar features, department history. Build them in an sklearn Pipeline so they're reproducible.
Train XGBoost baselines for all three tasks. Evaluate with time-based splits — never shuffle time series.
Compare against a naive seasonal baseline. If XGBoost doesn't beat it convincingly, say so — that honesty is the portfolio piece.
Serve as a FastAPI forecasting service: input date/hour horizon, output predictions with prediction intervals.
Add drift monitoring (Evidently, from your Post-ML stack): feature drift + prediction drift, alerts on threshold breach.
Simulate a drift event (shift the synthetic distribution) and show the alert firing plus your documented retrain response.
Write the README as an ops case study: baseline vs model, decision value of the improvement, drift playbook.
Record the demo: forecast vs actual on held-out weeks, drift alert firing, retrain flow.
Journal: where the model beat naive and where it didn't, and the operational decision each forecast would actually inform.

title: Phase 4 — Production & Governance
hours: ~30 hours · ship it safely, monitor it, prove it

weeks.title: Evaluation Platform & Portfolio Integration
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · the project that judges the others
weeks.mindset: An evaluation platform is the project that proves you understand all the others. It's Project 5 from the source path, promoted to capstone-adjacent status: shared eval datasets, hallucination tests, model comparison, human review — pointed at your own Projects 1–4.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday one deployed platform runs scheduled evals over your other projects and publishes a quality dashboard.

tasks.content: Design the platform: projects registry, eval datasets (gold sets from Projects 1–3), scheduled runs, results store, dashboard.
Define the metric menu per project type: RAG (precision@k, faithfulness), SQL (execution accuracy), agent (task success, gating compliance), forecasting (MAE vs naive).
Build the runner: pulls latest deploy of each project, executes its eval set, stores versioned results.
Add hallucination testing for the RAG project: unanswerable questions must yield refusals, not inventions. Score it.
Add model comparison: swap the RAG generator or the SQL model and get a side-by-side delta report per metric.
Add the human review queue: sampled outputs flagged for eyeballing, with reviewer verdicts stored.
Publish the dashboard: per-project quality over time, regression markers, links to the underlying runs.
Schedule nightly runs (cron/GitHub Action). A regression in any project opens an issue automatically.
Write the platform README: philosophy (evals as first-class), architecture, how to add a project.
Wire the platform link into your portfolio site next to each project.
Journal: which project evals caught a real regression this week — that story is your interview answer.

weeks.title: Production Hardening — Security & Monitoring
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · PHI boundaries, audit logs, alerting
weeks.mindset: Production healthcare AI is a security product with a model inside. Access control, PHI minimization, immutable audit logs, and honest monitoring are what distinguish a deployable system from a demo — and they're the first things a hospital security review will probe.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday all four portfolio services run hardened: auth, PHI-safe logging, audit trails, and live monitoring dashboards.

tasks.content: Add authentication + RBAC to every service: named roles (clinician, ops, admin) with least-privilege scopes.
Enforce PHI-safe logging: scrubbers for identifiers, structured logs with request ids, zero patient data in logs. Prove it with a grep test.
Centralize the audit trail: every prediction, retrieval, generation, approval, and admin action in one queryable store.
Write the audit query you'd hand a compliance officer: who saw what, when, under which role, for which patient encounter.
Stand up monitoring: service health, latency, error rates, model metrics (drift, eval scores) — Grafana or a simple metrics page.
Define alert rules with owners: drift breach, eval regression, error-rate spike, audit-write failure (the alert about alerts).
Run a threat-model pass on each service using OWASP LLM Top 10 (your Post-ML resource): prompt injection, data exfiltration via retrieval, privilege escalation.
Fix the top finding per service. Document the rest in a risk register with accepted/rejected decisions.
Write the production handbook for the whole portfolio: runbooks per service, rollback, incident response, model-update procedure.
Do a fire drill: kill a service, verify alerting, execute the rollback runbook, write the mock postmortem.
Journal: the threat-model finding that most changed your architecture, and the rollback drill time.

weeks.title: Capstone — Defense & Positioning
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · prove it, then tell the story
weeks.mindset: The finish line is not the code — it's the defense. Twelve weeks of systems, one recorded walkthrough, one honest retrospective, one positioning document. This is where the healthcare-operations veteran meets the AI engineer, on camera.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday a recorded 15-minute defense of the whole portfolio exists, plus the positioning one-pager, and the next 90 days are planned.

tasks.content: Run the full portfolio through the evaluation platform one final time. Screenshot everything — these numbers go in the defense.
Write the defense outline: system-by-system — problem, constraint, architecture, eval result, failure mode, what you'd change.
Record the 15-minute portfolio defense: live demos, honest numbers, the drift drill, the audit query. One take, minor edits only.
Publish it alongside the project repos and the eval dashboard links.
Write the positioning one-pager: healthcare operations + ERP integration + ML/GenAI engineering + governance. Target roles: healthcare AI engineer, clinical informatics engineer, AI adoption lead.
Update the portfolio site: certificates (ML Spec, Stanford AI in Healthcare), the five systems, the defense video.
Write the retrospective: strongest system, weakest system, the eval that saved you, the constraint that taught you most.
Publish it as a blog post — 'from hospital ERP engineer to healthcare AI engineer' is a story worth telling.
Plan the next 90 days: pick one real problem at work, scope it with the deployment-risk pack template, and propose it.
Decide the growth frontier: HL7 FHIR integration depth, clinical NLP papers, or health-system-scale MLOps.
Final journal entry: mark the track complete. Healthcare professional who understands AI engineering — and can prove it.
